strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: error slice discovery for instance-level vision tasks, where failures are often localized, relational, and not well captured by image-level clustering or attribute conjunctions.

The proposed generate-and-verify framing is conceptually appealing. Natural-language hypotheses, VLM-based instance grounding, and monotonic trend verification form an interpretable pipeline that is better matched to detection/segmentation failures than latent cluster discovery.

The new GESD benchmark is a potentially valuable contribution. It covers COCO, KITTI, and a face detection dataset, aggregates errors across several detectors/segmentation models, and provides spatially grounded expert-defined slices for both false positives and false negatives.

Empirical results are promising: GH-ESD improves detection-slice Precision@10 over HiBug2 by 0.10, leads across P@5/P@10/P@20, shows ablations for hypotheses, grounding, and verification, and includes evidence of downstream utility via model repair.
The paper is generally clear and well motivated, with useful examples distinguishing verified, unsupported, and spurious hypotheses.
weaknesses: The benchmark/evaluation protocol raises concerns about circularity and closed-world bias. GESD slices are expert-defined after inspecting aggregated model errors, and non-slice predictions are overwritten with ground truth, so evaluation focuses on known predefined slice types rather than open-ended discovery in realistic error distributions. This may overstate practical discovery performance.

The statistical verification module is weaker than its presentation suggests. The main method uses a maximum sliding-window slope with fixed thresholds, which can select favorable local trends and is vulnerable to multiple-testing effects across many generated hypotheses. The Spearman/FDR variant is mentioned, but the main results appear to rely on the less principled slope statistic.

Reproducibility is limited by dependence on proprietary or rapidly changing LLMs such as Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-5.2, substantial prompt-based components, and many details deferred to the supplement. It is unclear whether the benchmark annotations, generated hypotheses, prompts, matching scores, and code will be released in sufficient form to reproduce the results.

Baseline comparisons are not fully satisfying. Several methods are designed for image-level settings and require nontrivial adaptation; the paper does not convincingly separate gains from the proposed algorithm versus advantages from stronger prompt engineering, richer hypothesis descriptions, or the use of modern VLM/LLM backends.

The metric design is somewhat narrow. Precision@k over top retrieved samples emphasizes purity but gives limited information about coverage, duplicate/merged hypotheses, ranking quality across all slices, or performance on unknown failure modes. Hypothesis precision/recall is evaluated by an LLM judge, adding another subjective model-dependent layer.

The model repair evidence is encouraging but limited: the detection repair experiment appears to focus on a single bicycle slice/class, and broader repair results are mostly on standard classification bias benchmarks rather than the proposed instance-level benchmark. This leaves the claimed actionability only partially supported.

Dataset quality details are incomplete in the main paper, including annotator agreement, slice-size distributions, licensing considerations for the Kaggle face dataset, and how ambiguity in relational/spatial slice membership was resolved.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: instance-level error slice discovery for detection and segmentation, where image-level subgroup discovery is often too coarse. The emphasis on spatial grounding, relational/contextual failure descriptions, and model repair is well motivated for computer vision evaluation.

The proposed GESD benchmark, if released with full annotations and protocols, could be useful because existing slice-discovery benchmarks are mostly classification-oriented. The effort to annotate grounded false-positive/false-negative slices across COCO, KITTI, and a face dataset is potentially valuable.

The method is interpretable and practically oriented: natural-language hypotheses, VLM-based grounding, and trend-based verification produce slice descriptions that are easier to inspect than latent clusters. The paper also includes ablations and downstream repair experiments rather than only reporting discovery precision.
weaknesses: The central technical contribution is not very strong. GH-ESD is largely a pipeline combining LLM hypothesis generation, VLM yes/no scoring, and a simple monotonic trend filter. The paper does not convincingly establish that the specific algorithmic choices are principled or novel beyond prior language-driven/tag-driven slice discovery methods.

The statistical verification module is weakly justified. Using the maximum sliding-window regression slope can select spurious local trends under many tested hypotheses, and the main method lacks a clear multiple-testing correction, confidence intervals, calibration analysis, or null-baseline false-discovery study. The Spearman variant is mentioned, but the main retained statistic still appears vulnerable to cherry-picking over windows and generated hypotheses.

The benchmark construction risks circularity and limited generality. Expert-defined hypotheses are derived from aggregated model errors, and all non-slice predictions are overwritten by ground truth, creating a synthetic evaluation setting focused only on predefined known slices. This may reward methods that rediscover the annotation taxonomy rather than methods that discover open-world failures. Details on splits, leakage prevention, annotation agreement, slice sizes, and release/licensing are mostly deferred to supplementary material, which weakens the main paper's evidentiary case.

The evaluation metric is incomplete. Precision@k over top retrieved instances emphasizes purity but largely ignores coverage, duplicate/split hypotheses, and failure to recover many slices. The paper itself notes recall is hard, but then the main benchmark evidence relies heavily on P@k, making it difficult to judge whether GH-ESD discovers a comprehensive and useful set of failures.

Baseline comparisons are not fully convincing. Several baselines are image-level methods adapted in ways that may disadvantage them, while GH-ESD is purpose-built for the benchmark. The use of different LLM/VLM backends, unclear prompt sensitivity, and limited reporting of compute/cost/reproducibility make it hard to attribute gains specifically to the proposed framework rather than model choice or implementation details.

Claims of generalization to segmentation and model repair are under-supported in the main manuscript. Segmentation results are only referenced as supplementary baseline results, and the repair study focuses on a narrow bicycle slice plus standard classification benchmarks. This is not enough to substantiate broad claims that the discovered slices consistently enable actionable model improvements.

Reproducibility is a concern. The approach depends on proprietary or rapidly changing LLMs, generated hypotheses, prompts, and VLM logits, but the main text provides insufficient detail on deterministic settings, prompt variants, sampling, cost, and robustness across model versions. The GESD annotation protocol also needs stronger documentation to support independent reuse.

Overall, while the problem is worthwhile and the paper has some useful ingredients, the evidence does not overcome concerns about benchmark circularity, weak statistical validation, limited novelty, and potentially unfair/underspecified evaluation. I would lean toward rejection for ECCV in its current form.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: error slice discovery for instance-level vision tasks, where existing image-level clustering/tagging methods are often inadequate for localized, relational, and contextual failures.

The proposed GH-ESD formulation is conceptually strong. Generating interpretable natural-language hypotheses, grounding them with VLMs at the instance level, and statistically verifying monotonic error trends is a useful and coherent alternative to opaque embedding clusters or brittle tag conjunctions.

The new GESD benchmark is a significant contribution. It covers detection and segmentation failures across COCO, KITTI, and a face detection dataset, with expert-defined grounded slices and substantial annotation effort.

The empirical results are convincing overall: GH-ESD improves over adapted FACTS/HiBug/HiBug2 baselines on GESD, shows gains across FP/FN and error categories, includes ablations for hypotheses, grounding, and verification, and also demonstrates utility for model repair.
The paper is generally clear, well motivated, and positions the work well relative to prior slice discovery, bias discovery, and model debugging literature.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction may partly constrain the evaluation to predefined expert slices: non-slice predictions are overwritten by ground truth, which makes the benchmark clean but less representative of open-ended real deployment settings where unknown failure modes coexist with known slices.

The main verification statistic uses a max sliding-window slope with fixed thresholds, which can be sensitive to window selection and multiple hypothesis testing. The Spearman/FDR variant helps, but the main method would benefit from stronger statistical justification and clearer calibration procedures.

Reproducibility is somewhat limited by reliance on proprietary or rapidly changing LLM/VLM components such as Gemini and GPT-based baselines, plus prompt-dependent hypothesis generation. Runtime/cost details and robustness to model choice appear mostly deferred to the supplement.

The comparison to instance-level prior work is not fully exhaustive. VISLIX is discussed but not included experimentally, and several baselines require nontrivial adaptation, making some comparisons less clean than for native instance-level methods.

Segmentation evidence is comparatively weaker in the main paper, with key results relegated to the supplement. Given the paper claims support for detection and segmentation, more main-text segmentation analysis would strengthen the case.

Annotation quality details for GESD, such as inter-annotator agreement, disagreement resolution, and release/licensing specifics, are not sufficiently visible in the main paper despite being central to the dataset contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: instance-level error slice discovery for detection and segmentation, where image-level or attribute-conjunction methods are often inadequate for localized, relational, and contextual failures.

The proposed generate-and-verify framing is sensible and interpretable. Using LLMs to form candidate hypotheses, VLMs for grounded matching, and a statistical trend test to filter unsupported hypotheses is a coherent design that fits the problem well.

The new GESD benchmark is potentially valuable. It combines COCO, KITTI, and a face detection dataset, includes detection and segmentation failures, and provides spatially grounded expert slice definitions rather than only image-level subgroup labels.

Experimental results are reasonably broad: the paper compares against adapted slice-discovery baselines on GESD, evaluates image-level bias benchmarks, includes component ablations, studies VLM/LLM choices, and demonstrates a model-repair use case.
The method produces human-readable slice descriptions, which is a practical advantage over embedding-cluster approaches and important for model debugging workflows.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction raises concerns about evaluation circularity and realism. Expert slices are defined after analyzing aggregated model errors, and all non-slice errors are overwritten by ground truth. This creates a closed-world benchmark focused on predefined failures, which may overstate performance in real deployments where unknown and overlapping failure modes matter.

The main GESD metric, Precision@k against each ground-truth slice, does not adequately penalize excessive or spurious discovered hypotheses. The paper reports some semantic precision/recall using an LLM evaluator, but the central benchmark claim still rests heavily on top-k overlap and may not reflect full discovery quality.

Baseline comparisons are not fully satisfying. Most baselines are image-level methods adapted to an instance-level benchmark, while closer interactive or instance-level systems such as VISLIX are discussed but not empirically compared. The strength of the conclusion depends partly on whether the adapted baselines are the right reference points.

The statistical verification module is plausible but not fully rigorous. The max sliding-window slope can select favorable local trends, and although a Spearman variant and FDR correction are mentioned, the paper does not provide enough detail on hypothesis multiplicity, calibration of thresholds, or separation between hypothesis generation, threshold tuning, and final evaluation.

Segmentation evidence is weaker than the detection evidence: the supplement reports GH-ESD results on segmentation slices, but there is no comparable baseline table, making the claim of generalization to segmentation less convincing.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says GESD is publicly available but leaves the URL blank, and the pipeline depends on proprietary or rapidly changing LLMs as well as local VLM deployment. More complete release details, seeds, prompts, generated hypotheses, and annotation protocols are needed.

The model repair experiment is encouraging but narrow: the object detection repair focuses on a single bicycle slice, and the gains combine slice discovery with a GroupDRO-style training modification, so it is hard to isolate how generally actionable the discovered slices are.

Some claims are phrased more strongly than the evidence supports, especially around robustness to hallucination and benchmark standardization. The limitations section acknowledges open-ended hypothesis coverage, but the experiments do not deeply test failure cases where the hypothesis generator misses important slices or invents plausible but wrong ones.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: instance-level error slice discovery for detection and segmentation, where image-level slice discovery is indeed inadequate for many spatial, contextual, and relational failures.

The proposed framing of slice discovery as hypothesis generation plus grounded verification is intuitive and potentially useful. Natural-language hypotheses can express relational conditions that are hard to capture with atomic tags or embedding clusters.

GESD, if released with full annotations and protocols, could be a valuable benchmark. The paper reports substantial annotation effort and includes both detection and segmentation failure modes across COCO, KITTI, and a face detection dataset.
The experiments compare against several adapted slice discovery baselines, include ablations for hypotheses, grounding, and verification, and attempt to show downstream utility through model repair.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction creates serious evaluation concerns. Experts define the 21 detection and 21 segmentation slices from aggregated model errors, and then non-slice predictions are overwritten with ground truth. This produces a closed-world benchmark centered on predefined slices rather than realistic open-ended discovery, and it may substantially simplify the task in favor of methods that generate broad natural-language hypotheses.

The evaluation protocol appears overly permissive. Tables report the best predicted slice for each ground-truth slice and Precision@k of its top retrieved instances, but this does not sufficiently penalize redundant, excessive, or cherry-picked hypotheses. The paper itself notes that recall is difficult, yet the proposed semantic precision/recall is judged by an LLM evaluator, introducing another unvalidated model-dependent assessment.

The statistical verification module is not fully convincing. The main statistic is the maximum sliding-window slope after thresholding VLM scores, with fixed empirical parameters. Taking a maximum over windows and many generated hypotheses creates multiple-testing and selection-bias risks; the paper only partially addresses this with a supplementary Spearman variant, while the main results rely on the less principled statistic.

The claimed robustness against VLM hallucination is under-supported. Matching is based on yes/no token logits from Qwen2.5-VL, but there is little evidence that these scores are calibrated for grounded instance-level visual conditions, especially for subtle relational or contextual hypotheses.

Baseline adaptation may be unfair or incomplete. Several compared methods were designed for image-level settings and are adapted through image-level aggregation, while GH-ESD is designed directly for the instance-level benchmark. The paper does include HiBug-style baselines, but the comparison still leaves uncertainty about whether the gains reflect the core algorithm or benchmark/protocol alignment.

Reproducibility is weak in important places. The abstract says the dataset is publicly available but the URL is blank in the manuscript. The method depends on proprietary or changing LLM/VLM systems, interactive ChatGPT-generated attributes for baselines, and many prompt/model choices, making exact reproduction difficult.

The downstream repair evidence is narrow. The instance-level repair experiment focuses on one bicycle slice and one detector setup, so it does not strongly establish general practical impact for detection or segmentation model improvement.

The paper is clear at a high level, but many critical details are underspecified: how hypotheses are filtered before evaluation, whether test-time data are used to construct data-driven hypotheses, how annotation consistency was measured, how many candidate hypotheses are generated per task, and how failure cases are handled beyond a few examples. These omissions weaken confidence in the empirical case.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely gap: error slice discovery for instance-level tasks such as detection and segmentation, where image-level clusters or atomic attributes are often inadequate. The framing around grounded, relational hypotheses is well motivated and relevant to computer vision evaluation and robustness.

GH-ESD is conceptually appealing: it combines LLM-generated hypotheses, region-grounded VLM matching, and statistical verification of error trends. The continuous matching-score formulation is a useful improvement over hard slice membership and supports more nuanced instance-level analysis.

The new GESD benchmark is a valuable contribution. It includes expert-defined, spatially grounded detection and segmentation error slices across COCO, KITTI, and a face-detection dataset, with nontrivial annotation effort and a clear attempt to evaluate realistic model failures.

Empirical results are strong on the proposed benchmark: GH-ESD improves detection Precision@10 over the strongest HiBug2 baseline by 0.10 and performs well across false positives, false negatives, and different error categories. The supplementary segmentation results further suggest the approach is not limited to boxes.

The ablations are meaningful and support the main design choices: natural-language hypotheses outperform atomic tags in semantic alignment, instance-level grounding improves over image-level aggregation, and monotonic verification improves robustness relative to simple error-rate thresholding.

The paper also evaluates generalization to image-level bias benchmarks and includes model repair experiments, which strengthen the claim that discovered slices are actionable rather than merely descriptive.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction raises some concerns about evaluation realism and possible bias. GESD ground-truth slices are expert-defined from an aggregated error pool, and all non-slice predictions are overwritten by ground truth. This creates a clean testbed, but also a partly synthetic setting that may overemphasize predefined known failures and underrepresent open-world unknown slices.

Evaluation relies heavily on Precision@k, mostly P@10. This is consistent with prior work, but it gives an incomplete picture of discovery quality, especially since generated hypotheses may split or merge slices. The paper provides some hypothesis precision/recall analysis, but the main benchmark would be stronger with more systematic coverage, recall, and false-discovery analyses.

The statistical verification module is intuitive but not fully rigorous as presented. Using the maximum sliding-window slope can inflate positives through multiple comparisons, and thresholds such as gamma=0.5 and tau=0.2 are empirical. The Spearman/FDR variant in the supplement helps, but the main method still needs clearer calibration and uncertainty treatment.

Some baseline comparisons may disadvantage prior methods because several are adapted from image-level settings, while GH-ESD is designed for instance-level grounding. The paper makes reasonable adaptations, but the fairness of comparing against FACTS*/HiBug* under image-level aggregation or tag-conjunction constraints remains only partially resolved.

Reproducibility depends on powerful proprietary or rapidly changing LLM/VLM components, including Gemini/GPT variants, and the public availability statement in the abstract appears incomplete. The prompts are included, but code, exact generated hypotheses, dataset release details, and model outputs are important for reproducing the benchmark claims.

The practical repair evidence is promising but narrow. The object-detection repair experiment centers on one bicycle slice, and the classification repair uses different repair protocols for different methods. This supports actionability but does not yet establish broad, reliable repair benefits across many discovered slices and detection categories.
